item.title: The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
item.description:
The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

item.title: American Express layoffs: Thousands of roles slashed in AI push as job losses in financial services pile up
item.description:
It hasn’t been a good week for workers in the banking and financial sector. Yesterday, UK banking giant Barclays announced it was laying off 5% of its workforce, or nearly 5,000 workers, as it transitions more of the bank’s operations to artificial intelligence systems.

Across the Atlantic this morning, an American financial giant made a similar announcement.

The American Express Company (NYSE: AXP), owner of the eponymous credit card and associated financial services, announced that it will slash 5% of its workforce due to AI. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

On Friday morning, American Express CEO Stephen Squeri announced that the U.S. financial giant was eliminating 5% of its global workforce.

American Express had roughly 76,800 employees at the end of 2025, so a 5% reduction equates to about 3,840 job losses.

Amex confirmed the layoffs to Fast Company when reached for comment.

“We’ve got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we need to become a more agile and efficient organization,” American Express CEO Steve Squeri said on a call this morning with analysts.

Squeri added: “When completed, we believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities.”

And yes, artificial intelligence is one of the facets driving the layoffs.

American Express chief financial officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC that the restructuring in part would help the company “to prepare for AI.”

“You don’t want to automate processes that are not optimally structured, and so what we’re doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years,” Le Caillec told the network.

American Express stock falls

Following the layoff news, American Express’s stock price fell—but likely not because the company announced layoffs. 

Despite the harm to the individual losing their jobs, Wall Street generally cheers job cuts because they are the fastest way for companies to reduce spending and thus increase their bottom line.

The cuts were announced alongside Amex’s Q3 2026 results today. Those results saw the financial giant report record third-quarter revenue of $20.1 billion, which was up 9% year-over-year. Net income reached $3.7 billion, up from $2.9 billion a year earlier.

Yet the company’s stock price is currently trading down around 3% in early morning trading, likely related to a general fall in markets as Brent crude reaches a six-month high amid the ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran.

Year to date, AXP has now fallen around 13%.

As Fast Company reported yesterday, Barclays—and now American Express—are not the only banking giants that have cut jobs in 2026.

Both Citigroup and HSBC cut 10% of their workforces earlier this year. Standard Chartered said it will cut 15% of its workforce by 2030.

item.title: Europe’s brutally hot summer led to more than 50,000 heat deaths in urban areas alone
item.description:
The summer of 2026 was brutally hot across Europe, with five successive heat waves causing record-high temperatures across the continent. 

Those extremes likely led to more than 50,000 excess deaths in urban areas alone, according to a new estimate.

And some 32,000 of those deaths, or nearly two-thirds of that total, can be directly attributed to climate change, caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

This makes the summer of 2026 likely the “worst on record” for heat-related deaths across much of Europe, according to Clair Barnes, a study author and extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College London.

Dangers of extreme heat

The figures come from two recent studies published in the journal Nature Health.

Researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine looked at 854 urban areas across 30 countries (27 of which are in the European Union, plus the UK, Norway and Switzerland). Those areas account for 40% of those countries’ total population. 

By using temperature records combined with climate modeling, they were able to estimate how many excess heat-related deaths occurred every summer between 2000 and 2026. Where governments have released official mortality statistics, these findings align with official figures, the researchers say.

Heat death can be difficult to measure. Heat itself often isn’t listed as a cause of death on death certificates, except in certain instances of heat stroke.

But only counting heat strokes is a “vast underestimation of the actual effect” of extreme heat, says Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, a study author and assistant professor at Imperial College London. 

Heat is one of the deadliest climate change impacts. Extreme heat stresses our cardiovascular and metabolic systems, and can combine with other illnesses to exacerbate health harms. 

This is why this count of excess deaths is an estimate, the researchers note. For the summer of 2026, many countries haven’t yet released their official mortality numbers.

Where they have, though, the researchers’ model estimates align with those figures. The researchers estimated, for example, that May and June heat waves in England and Wales caused more than 2,700 deaths. An analysis by the UK Health Security Agency later identified about 2,880 deaths in that time period. 

The role of climate change

The studies also specifically looked at the role of climate change in these deaths by modeling a pre-industrial world in which human-caused climate change didn’t happen.

Even in that world, temperatures were so dangerously hot that they led to high deaths, Barnes says. 

“But that mortality has been pushed substantially higher by human-caused warming, primarily from the burning of fossil fuels,” she adds. “Across Europe as a whole, around two thirds of those deaths would not have occurred without the additional heat from human activity.” 

Temperatures for that entire summer were 2.9°C above the prior decade’s average. Some days were so hot that they hit 12°C above average. 

The summer of 2026 saw the highest number of urban heat deaths in all 26 years the researchers analyzed. The summer of 2022, which was also marred by multiple dangerous heat waves, was second, with about 29,000 deaths. 

Climate change is warming the entire planet, but Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Over the summer, multiple European governments issued “red weather warnings” about the heat, even closing schools and canceling sports events. 

“These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health. Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them,” Barnes says. 

And they’re also a reminder, she adds, “of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

item.title: The New Energy Stalemate in Ukraine
item.description: Tatiana Mitrova, a fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and former energy scholar at Moscow’s Russian Academy of Sciences, and Sergey Vakulenko, an oil and gas expert at Carnegie’s Russia Eurasia Center, argue that Russia and Ukraine are locked in an energy war that has become an adaptation spiral, despite growing human and economic costs and despite current US pressure on Ukraine. They observe Ukraine’s remarkable ability to withstand Russian strikes, while questioning claims that long-range Ukrainian strikes will be able to achieve game-changing damage on Russia. Ukraine and Russia have transformed the role of energy warfare in modern conflict, drawing on low costs drones but also new forms of technological resilience that are likely to make wars longer and more dangerous.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks
item.description:
Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday. In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.

The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.

The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.

The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort. EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine.

The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trilateral peace talks with Russia to restart, says Zelenskyy
item.description:
Ukraine will not discuss limits to its armed forces or enforced neutrality at November meeting, president says. What we know on day 1,706

A trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow will take place in November aiming to restart stalled Russia-Ukraine peace talks, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. “We are ready to talk. If it’s a territorial issue, it must be addressed at a leadership level. Other issues fall within the remit of the technical groups. All this can therefore be discussed in November,” the Ukrainian president said on Sunday in an interview. Zelenskyy also renewed his push ⁠for a meeting between him and Vladimir Putin, believing that Putin is the only person ​in Russia who can make major decisions to end ​the war.

Zelenskyy says that at the trilateral talks, Ukraine will not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced postwar neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into Nato despite the reticence of some members.

Meanwhile, US warnings about imminent ⁠Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, have been fully restored, according to Zelenskyy. He told Ukraine’s ⁠TSN television channel that SpaceX’s ​Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420km/h since early on Saturday, after a meeting with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo. Starshield was throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.

The US has been trying to pressure Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it says push energy prices higher. However, Zelenskyy has repeatedly said Kyiv will only stop the strikes if Moscow stops hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or if the US allows Ukraine to use of Starshield ‌over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or if it supplies Ukraine with Patriot missiles.

Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post.

Russia’s defence ⁠ministry said on ⁠Sunday ​its drones had struck a ⁠cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of ⁠Chornomorsk in an overnight ​attack ‌and another cargo ‌vessel en route to the ‌port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian ‌forces also hit a logistics centre, a ​distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. Reuters could not confirm the reports.

A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city ⁠of Belgorod killed ⁠three people ​and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while ⁠a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person. The overnight attack on Belgorod ​damaged 30 apartment buildings, regional governor ⁠Alexander Shuvayev said.

The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova. Iotova opposes military aid to Ukraine and favours dialogue with Russia, while Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Kyiv. The vote was held amid security concerns after a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.

item.title: How the Fed is likely to act on interest rates just days before the midterm elections
item.description:
The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates Wednesday even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices.

The Fed’s latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items.

The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation.

Yet Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.

At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.

After the Fed announces its rate decision, Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed’s next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed’s desire for a “timelier” return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors.

If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.

And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed’s 2% target.

On Thursday, a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.

Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy.

“Unless the Fed takes this problem more seriously and stops essentially making excuses about inflation, I think we’re not going to get back to 2% until the next recession,” Bhave said.

Warsh will likely seek to keep the Wednesday press conference relatively short. It was about 30 minutes last month. Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, often held news conferences for about 45 minutes.

The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.

For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.

Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren’t particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

—Christopher Rugaber, AP Economics Writer

item.title: Google and Apple hit with a combined fine of $47.6 million by South Korea’s watchdog
item.description:
South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet’s Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country’s media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.

Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

—Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce holding and demining under way to enable humanitarian corridor, Kyiv says
item.description:
No reported incidents in 30 hours in the occupied Ukrainian city. What we know on day 1,709

A local ceasefire in southern Ukraine was holding for a second day, both sides said on Wednesday, as hopes grew that vital aid would be able to reach stranded residents. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region amid food and medical shortages and reports many people are now starving and eating weeds. The human rights ombudsmen of both Russia and Ukraine said on Wednesday the US-brokered truce – which came into effect early on Tuesday morning – was still holding. “30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky have passed without a single incident,” Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets said. “No incidents have been recorded in the 30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky,” Russia’s Yana Lantratova said in a similarly worded statement. The ceasefire would be guaranteed by “the physical presence of both ombudsmen: Ukrainian and Russian” on the ground, Lubinets’s office said. Route demining was “currently under way”, Lubinets said on social media, describing it as “crucial step toward ensuring the safe delivery of humanitarian aid and enabling civilians who wish to leave the city”.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that since the ceasefire came into force, there had been “no massive attacks” on the regional capital of Kherson, where about 280,000 people lived before Russia’s invasion. “We’re happy even when we have two, three days for these people. You know, some ceasefire is great, you can see them in the streets,” the Ukrainian president told reporters in The Hague. The truce would be a “huge success” if the evacuation of Oleshky’s citizens went ahead as planned, he said.

The timing of the next round of three-way ⁠talks on a settlement of the Ukraine conflict is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, a Kremlin foreign policy aide has said, casting doubt on whether the talks will take place next month as initially proposed. Yuri Ushakov, quoted by Russian news ⁠agencies, said Moscow had not yet proposed a specific date for the talks. “It will ​also depend on the situation ‌on the battlefield and the ‌situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It ‌just doesn’t allow us to hold it in the near future. That’s my assumption,” he told journalists on Wednesday. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between 6 and 10 November.

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s “genius” and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine, reports Dan Sabbagh. The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation. “Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Tass news agency quoted the Russian leader as saying.

The Netherlands will supply Ukraine with €500m ($557m/£418m) ⁠in military support ⁠this ​winter, the Dutch prime minister said. The support ⁠would be used to supply drones and other material to ⁠strengthen Ukraine’s defence, Rob Jetten said ​after meeting Zelenskyy in The Hague. Earlier on ‌Wednesday, the Dutch government announced it would give Kyiv €1.2bn in non-military support in the next three years. Part of the money would be used for funds that supported ⁠Dutch companies willing to invest in the ​rebuilding ​of Ukraine.

Russian authorities have issued permits for ⁠vessels carrying grain for export to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since 10 July, ⁠when they closed maritime ⁠traffic ​in the area due to Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters quoted seven industry sources as saying. item.title: The Trump administration is now blacklisting this major biotech company and its affiliates. Here’s why
item.description:
The Trump administration said Wednesday that it is blocking shipments by the Chinese biotech company BGI Group and its affiliates, alleging ties to forced labor in China’s far-west ethnic region of Xinjiang.

Starting Thursday, U.S. Customs and Border Protection will bar goods by BGI Group, a major biotech company known for its genetic sequencing technologies, as well as BGI Genomics and MGI Tech. The Department of Homeland Security said the companies are either sourcing materials from Xinjiang or working with the regional government to “recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor” of members of persecuted ethnic groups in Xinjiang, including Uyghurs.

Adding the companies to a trade blacklist comes as biotechnology is emerging as another front in the economic and tech competition between the U.S. and China. The Treasury Department last week proposed new restrictions on U.S. investments in biotechnology, artificial intelligence and supercomputing from flowing into countries such as China.

China said it rejected any accusation of forced labor and called the ban an act of “political manipulation” and “bullying under the guise of ‘protecting human rights.'”

“These listings run counter to the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state, seriously undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and violate the spirit of humanitarianism,” said China’s Ministry of Commerce in a Thursday morning statement. “China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its interests.”

The latest trade actions precede an expected meeting next month between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where BGI Group is based. Xi could then travel to Florida in December for the Group of 20 leaders summit and meet Trump for the fourth time this year as the two try to keep ties stable during a trade truce.

BGI Group rejected the allegations, saying in a statement Wednesday that it “has not engaged in any form of forced labor.” It added that “we firmly oppose all forms of forced labor.”

The company has controlling stakes in BGI Genomics and MGI Tech, DHS said.

BGI Group has for several years been a concern to U.S. lawmakers and policymakers, who are worried that its alleged ties to the Chinese government and access to massive genetic data could hurt U.S. national security and commercial interests. The company has long stressed its private ownership and said it does not serve patients in the U.S. and has no access to Americans’ genetic data.

While Congress failed to pass legislation banning BGI from doing business with federally funded medical providers, it passed a similar provision at the end of last year without naming specific companies. It asked for a list of “biotechnology companies of concerns” to be compiled.

The Pentagon has labeled BGI Group, BGI Genomics and MGI Tech as Chinese military companies, a designation that carries reputational damage.

In its announcement Wednesday, DHS pointed to “credible information, including corporate and government reporting” showing that BGI Group, BGI Genomics and MGI Tech have supported genetic testing in Xinjiang.

“The collection and analysis of genetic material facilitate the monitoring, surveillance, and repression of ethnic minorities by the government of the People’s Republic of China, including the abhorrent practice of forced labor,” the department said.

The new restrictions are part of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which then-President Joe Biden signed into law at the end of 2021 following allegations of human rights abuses by Beijing against members of the ethnic Uyghur group and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.

The Chinese government has refuted the claims as lies and defended its practice and policy in Xinjiang as fighting terror and ensuring stability.

In August, the Trump administration drastically expanded the blacklist under that law to include 43 Chinese companies, for a total of 187 entities. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has vowed to protect American workers from getting undercut or cheated by foreign companies using “slave labor.”
—
AP writer Huizhong Wu contributed to this report.

—Didi Tang, Associated Press

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Outrage in Europe after Russian drone kills 14 on rail platform in Dnipro
item.description:
EU council president calls deadly strike ‘cruel and devastating’; fragile ceasefire holds in Oleshky. What we know on day 1,710

European leaders have reacted with outrage to a deadly attack by a Russian drone that slammed into a busy railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Ukraine had intelligence about more ballistic missile strikes to come. French President Emmanuel Macron stressed the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire”, referencing the current truce in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The EU council president, António Costa, who described the Dnipro attacks as “cruel and devastating”, called for greater pressure on Russia after the latest strikes against civilians. “The EU will continue to increase the pressure on Russia and to support Ukraine until a just and lasting peace is achieved,” he added. “We call on all our international partners to do the same.”

Later on Thursday, Russian forces ⁠launched ⁠an attack ​on the ⁠Ukrainian capital ⁠Kyiv ​with ‌ballistic ‌missiles, Mayor Vitali Klitschko ‌said on Telegram, hitting warehouses and ‌triggering a fire. Emergency services were headed to ​the scene on the east side ⁠of the Dnipro ​River, he said.

Describing the Dnipro train station attack – which killed at least 14 people and injured another 14 – as “horrific”, the president of Ukraine insisted “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”. Zelenskyy warned also that Ukraine had intelligence about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. “We need the means to take out all this Russian ‌evil. We are expecting relevant decisions,” he said. Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, adding the assaults had cut power to 350,000 households.

The strikes came as Ukraine and Russia kept to a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages. While the truce held into a third day, strikes elsewhere in Ukraine killed at least 20 people and injured more than 70 people, according to local officials. Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday an operation to bring aid into the town and allow ⁠residents to leave was ready to begin.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military ⁠has paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump, ⁠according to a report in the Wall Street ⁠Journal ​on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations. Ukrainian units carrying out ⁠long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once ⁠missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported. The ​unofficial pause is expected ‌to last until ‌after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into ‌November, the newspaper said.

After the Dnipro attack, Zelenskyy renewed his criticism of a deal struck between Trump and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin to ease some US sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel on to global markets. “How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating?” he asked.

Late on Thursday, Putin said he supported any steps aimed at restoring relations with ⁠European countries, saying the outbreak of any conflict would leave ⁠a situation with ⁠no ​winners. Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin told reporters after ‌hosting a summit with African ‌leaders: “And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. .”

item.title: Carney targets June deadline to finalize Canada’s historic EU associate membership
item.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Friday he expects to conclude negotiations with the European Union in June on an unprecedented partnership that would make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member,” even though the designation was left out of a joint declaration launching a new economic and security alliance.

Carney said he would attend a meeting of European leaders in June to conclude negotiations on the proposed relationship, which would stop short of full EU membership.

“In parallel, we are working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession—with Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member,” Carney said.

The joint declaration issued at the end of a two-day summit in Montreal made no mention of associate membership. Instead, the leaders agreed to define an “ever-closer association” by their next summit in 2027.

European Council President António Costa said the alliance would be the closest relationship the EU has ever established with a country outside the bloc, expanding cooperation on trade, research, and security as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war strains relations with traditional allies.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said shared values mattered more than geography in determining which countries should work together.

“It is not so important where the countries are on the map,” von der Leyen said. “What is important are the values that a country defends and where countries stand in international relations.”

Carney said the proposed alliance would strengthen the sovereignty of Canada and Europe and help them weather economic shocks.

“And it means, at its base, sovereignty, greater resilience, an ability to withstand shocks together,” he said.

Von der Leyen has been pushing for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member,” despite resistance from some European governments to the designation. Carney has also used the term, although he has emphasized that the partnership’s benefits matter more than its name.

“We want Canada as close a partner as possible to the European Union,” von der Leyen said. “We know that Canada cannot be a full-fledged member of the European Union, but to have a relationship as close as possible, this is our goal.”

Carney said the proposed alliance would make life more affordable, give consumers more choices, and create opportunities for businesses, young people, and researchers.

Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU were also creating a common space with other trusted partners to confront challenges involving critical minerals, resilient supply chains, artificial intelligence, and space.

The leaders are expected to announce a digital trade agreement Friday, along with initiatives to expand scientific research partnerships and university student exchanges. Von der Leyen has also said the two sides would finalize an agreement giving Canadian companies and researchers access to Europe’s network of supercomputers to develop artificial intelligence.

Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025, underscoring the challenge Carney faces as he seeks to double exports to other countries over the next decade.

item.title: Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
item.description:
The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”
